svg.title: The route distinguisher: how eight bytes turn IPv4 into VPNv4, and why it must be unique per PE
svg.desc: Upper panel shows the conversion: an IPv4 prefix of four bytes gains an eight-byte route distinguisher in front to become a twelve-byte VPNv4 prefix, so two customers with the identical 10.1.0.0/16 produce two different VPNv4 routes. Middle panel gives three allocation models: type 0 with a two-byte AS number and four-byte number, type 1 with a four-byte IP address and two-byte number, and type 2 with a four-byte AS and two-byte number. Lower panel shows the multihoming case: a dual-homed site advertised by two PEs which use the same RD produces one VPNv4 prefix with two paths, so only one is selected; with a unique RD per PE the two become distinct prefixes and both can be installed, which is what makes active-active multihoming possible. A closing note states the rule: RD identifies the advertising router, not the customer.
svg.text: Eight bytes in front of the prefix: the only thing preventing a global address collision
RD makes routes unique; RT decides who may use them. Confusing the two is the most common L3VPN error
IPv4 BECOMES VPNv4 BY PREPENDING THE RD
4 bytes · not unique in the world
8 bytes · unique per VRF or per PE
12 bytes · globally unique VPNv4 route
Two customers, the same 10.1.0.0/16, two
different RDs → two distinct routes in
BGP. Without the RD the second would
THREE FORMATS, ALL EIGHT BYTES
Type 0: 2-byte AS : 4-byte number → 65000:1
Type 1: 4-byte IP : 2-byte number → 192.0.2.1:1
Type 2: 4-byte AS : 2-byte number → 4200000001:1
Type 1 uses the loopback address, so it is stable if the AS number changes.
Whichever you choose, write it down per VRF: a duplicate RD is silent until it is not.
WHY UNIQUENESS PER PE MATTERS: MULTIHOMING
Same RD on both PEs: both advertise 65000:1 10.1.0.0/16.
BGP sees one prefix with two paths → best-path picks one.
The second link carries nothing. Not a bug, just maths.
Unique RD per PE: 65000:1 and 65000:2 → two routes.
Both install, so active-active multihoming and per-flow hashing work.
The rule: an RD represents the advertising PE (or VRF on that PE), not the customer. A customer-facing identifier belongs in the RT, where policy can read it.
Practical default: one RD per VRF per PE, derived from the PE loopback, and recorded in the VRF table of the design document alongside the RTs.
Failure signature to memorise: a prefix from the wrong customer appears in a VRF. The RD was reused across two customers, so one route
overwrote the other and the surviving one was imported by an RT that happened to match. RD first, RT second, always in that order.
